summary: Background: Emergency departments (EDs) are vital access points for urgent care, yet persistent overcrowding in health care systems worldwide compromises service quality and efficiency. Urban tertiary care centers are increasingly strained by surging patient numbers and scarce inpatient beds. Prior admission prediction studies mostly rely on limited triage features and discrimination metrics, neglecting operational factors, calibration, and explainability. Identifying likely admissions early could enable proactive resource allocation and shorter wait times. Objective: This study aimed to develop and evaluate machine learning models for predicting hospital admission at the end of triage using routinely collected structured data while addressing prior limitations regarding feature selection, model calibration, and explainability. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adult ED visits between January 2015 and December 2022 at 2 academic hospitals in the McGill University Health Centre. We excluded visits with dispositions other than admission or discharge to ensure a binary outcome. Data were split into training (70%), validation (10%), and testing (20%) sets using stratified random sampling. We trained classifiers, including logistic regression (LR), decision trees, random forests, artificial neural networks, and gradient boosting algorithms (extreme gradient boosting [XGBoost], light gradient boosting machine, and categorical boosting), using demographics, vital signs, chief complaints, comorbidities, and historical hospitalization frequency available at triage. Sensitivity analyses tested exclusion criteria and temporal data shifts, while subgroup analyses examined differences by age, sex, and site. Performance was evaluated using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC), sensitivity, specificity, and calibration. We also performed a decision threshold analysis to assess operational flexibility and used Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) values to interpret feature contributions. Results: The final cohort included 526,145 visits (mean age 50.9, SD 21.1 years; 272,767/526,145, 51.8% female), with 91,363 patients (17.4%) admitted. The XGBoost model achieved the highest performance, with an AUC-ROC of 0.86 (95% CI 0.858‐0.864), a sensitivity of 0.67, and a specificity of 0.86, outperforming the LR baseline (AUC 0.84). Key predictors identified by SHAP values included age, Canadian Triage and Acuity Scale scores, arrival mode, and historical hospitalization frequency. Subgroup analyses confirmed strong performance across age, sex, and sites. Sensitivity analyses evaluating alternative outcome dispositions and chronological data splits confirmed overall model stability. Threshold analysis showed that adjusting the decision threshold to the 0.70 to 0.75 range improved the positive predictive value and did not disproportionately reclassify older or higher-acuity patients. Conclusions: In urban tertiary care settings, structured triage data available at triage can effectively anticipate hospital admissions. By incorporating broad feature sets and operational variables, models such as XGBoost offer a feasible, explainable tool for early decision-making. Such tools could improve coordination between emergency and inpatient services and ease overcrowding. Future work should prioritize prospective validation and real-time clinical workflow integration.
title: Explainable Machine Learning for Predicting Hospital Admission at Emergency Department Triage: Retrospective Cohort Study

summary: Background: Clinical documentation is a major contributor to physician workload and burnout, particularly in high-acuity settings such as emergency departments. Ambient AI scribes have emerged as a response, but commercial products cost US $99 to more than US $600 per physician per month, operate as opaque systems, and often process data on vendor-controlled infrastructure. These characteristics limit organizational control over data sovereignty, quality improvement, and clinical workflows and create barriers to adoption in resource-constrained settings. Objective: We aimed to develop an open-source, modular AI scribe platform that could be deployed entirely within institutional infrastructure, and to evaluate its real-world use across a provincial health system. Methods: We developed Berta, an open-source, modular platform that pairs a Next.js front end and a FastAPI back end with configurable automatic speech recognition and large language model components. A closed-source implementation developed in parallel with Berta was deployed at Alberta Health Services (AHS), Canada’s largest provincially integrated health system at the time of implementation, and operated within AHS’s existing Snowflake AI Data Cloud infrastructure. All clinical audio and text remained within the secure AHS environment. Use and session metadata were automatically recorded during routine clinical use by emergency physicians across AHS between November 2024 and July 2025, and physicians were emailed an optional survey. Operating costs were estimated from Snowflake service consumption over the same period. Implementation (Results): During the 9-month study period, 197 emergency physicians registered at 105 urban and rural facilities used the system, generating 21,548 clinical sessions and more than 2700 hours of audio. Monthly session volume grew from 675 sessions in November 2024 to 5463 in July 2025. Mean recorded session length was 7.6 minutes, and 42% (82/197) of users customized at least 1 documentation template. Operating costs averaged less than US $30 per physician per month, representing a 70% to 95% reduction in cost compared with commercial subscription prices; this comparison excludes personnel costs for development and maintenance. Survey respondents (69-73 per item) rated user-friendliness as good (median 5, IQR 4-6), reported a median time saving of 16 to 30 (IQR 0-15 to 46-60) minutes per shift, and rated documentation quality the lowest. After the pilot, access was opened to other departments, and by September 30, 2026, approximately 2000 users had registered. Conclusions: An in-house AI scribe can be deployed at provincial scale within existing health system infrastructure at a fraction of the operating cost of commercial alternatives while preserving data sovereignty and institutional control. The full cost of ownership and documentation quality require further evaluation. By releasing Berta publicly, we provide a reproducible foundation that health systems can adapt to evaluate and deploy AI documentation technology within their own secure environments.
title: Berta, an Open-Source, Modular AI Scribe for Clinical Documentation: Implementation Report

summary: Background: Demand for health data to support research, innovation, and evidence-based policymaking is increasing, but access to patient-level data is constrained by privacy and data protection requirements. To address this challenge, the Czech Republic developed a national synthetic data infrastructure within the National Health Information System (NHIS). The infrastructure aims to support privacy-preserving secondary use of health data by enabling the development and validation of analytical workflows without providing direct access to operational patient-level databases. Objective: This study describes the design, implementation, governance framework, and operational evaluation of the Czech NHIS synthetic data infrastructure as a national platform for privacy-preserving secondary use of health data and for the development of reproducible analytical workflows. The system strongly supports the continuing relevance and importance of national infrastructures during the transition to full European Health Data Space (EHDS) implementation. Methods: The infrastructure was implemented using selected nationwide registries, including reimbursement, cancer, reproductive health, and mortality databases. Synthetic datasets were generated using registry-specific rule-based procedures designed to preserve database structures, variable formats, and selected longitudinal relationships while preventing reconstruction of real patient records. Researchers developed and tested SQL-based analytical workflows within the synthetic environment, whereas execution on primary NHIS databases and disclosure control review were performed exclusively by authorized personnel. The implementation was evaluated using predefined operational indicators, including user adoption, request volume, processing outcomes, transparency measures, and privacy-related incidents. Implementation (Results): The infrastructure enables the development and validation of SQL-based analytical workflows without direct access to primary patient-level data. Synthetic datasets representing approximately 0.04% to 0.26% of the selected NHIS registries were created while maintaining schema compatibility and selected analytical relationships. Between the platform’s public launch and July 23, 2026, a total of 170 users registered, 199 requests were submitted, and 184 requests have been processed (173 with data delivery). A total of 41 (20.6%) requests included consent to share SQL scripts, thereby supporting public transparency and reproducibility. Practical implementation was demonstrated through operational use cases in oncology, nephrology, cardiology, and vaccination research. No privacy-related incidents were reported during the evaluation period. Conclusions: The Czech NHIS synthetic data infrastructure demonstrates that privacy-preserving secondary use of national health data can be implemented through a General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)–aligned governance framework that combines synthetic data, controlled execution on operational databases, disclosure-risk assessment, and transparent analytical workflows. Rather than serving as a statistically valid surrogate for inferential research, the infrastructure supports the reproducible development of workflows and the secure preparation of population-level analyses. As a fully operational national implementation aligned with the principles of the EHDS, the platform may provide a reference model for other countries developing privacy-preserving health data ecosystems.
title: Implementation of a National Synthetic Data Infrastructure for Privacy-Preserving Analytical Workflows in the Czech National Health Information System: Development and Evaluation Study

summary: Background: Heart failure develops through complex longitudinal interactions among multiple chronic diseases, making longitudinal disease trajectories an important source of clinical information. Longitudinal disease trajectories contain rich structural information that reflects disease evolution and comorbidity interactions. However, this information is often lost when electronic health record (EHR) data are summarized using conventional pooling strategies or sparse International Classification of Diseases (ICD) representations. Objective: This study aimed to develop an interpretable trajectory representation that preserves structural characteristics of longitudinal disease evolution for heart failure risk stratification using EHRs. Methods: Longitudinal ICD trajectories were represented using Node2Vec embeddings and summarized with information gain (IG)–weighted geometric features, including historical means, directional shifts, dispersion, and deviation relative to high-risk disease representations. The resulting maximum IG-weighted deviation geometric (mIGwDG) representation was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation against conventional embedding aggregation strategies, sparse ICD one-hot encoding, and a long short-term memory (LSTM) model. To facilitate interpretation of longitudinal disease evolution, we further developed a risk-aware pseudotime framework to organize patient trajectories along a model-inferred risk continuum and used a framework combining IG with the positive pointwise mutual information (PPMI) framework to characterize clinically relevant comorbidity patterns. Results: The proposed framework achieved an out-of-fold (OOF) area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) of 0.667 and an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.888, outperforming conventional embedding aggregation methods. Compared with sparse ICD one-hot encoding, the proposed framework reduced feature dimensionality by approximately 75% while maintaining comparable predictive performance. Combining mIGwDG with sparse ICD one-hot features further improved both logistic regression (LR) and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), suggesting that the proposed representation captures complementary longitudinal disease trajectory information. In addition, the risk-aware pseudotime framework organized heterogeneous patient trajectories along a model-inferred risk continuum, while IG×PPMI analysis highlighted clinically relevant comorbidity patterns that supported the interpretation of longitudinal disease organization. Conclusions: The proposed framework provides a compact and interpretable representation of longitudinal disease trajectories while maintaining comparable predictive performance. By combining geometric trajectory characterization with risk-aware pseudotime visualization, the framework facilitates the representation of longitudinal EHRs, the visualization of disease evolution, and risk stratification.
title: A Disease Trajectory Representation Framework With Risk-Aware Pseudotime Analysis for Electronic Health Records: Application to Heart Failure Risk Stratification

summary: Background: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for health information, but chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)–related questions often involve safety-sensitive decisions, including treatment escalation, oxygen therapy, and exacerbation management. Because generative outputs may vary across repeated prompts, response stability is also relevant to comparative evaluation. Objective: This study aims to compare 6 public-facing LLM chatbots in answering COPD-related public health questions across safety, accuracy, empathy, information quality, source transparency, readability, and 2-round response stability. Methods: We developed a 55-question English COPD question bank from an initial 108-question pool using web-based retrieval, Google Trends, PubMed-informed topic review, patient education resources, and expert screening. Six public-facing chatbot products were evaluated in a primary first round and a post hoc independent second round, added after first-round data collection, using the same 55 questions. Visible model/mode labels are provided in the supplementary materials. Five blinded raters assessed manually scored outcomes against a Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) 2026-centered reference standard, and 6 readability indices were calculated. The primary cross-model analysis used the first round; the second round was analyzed as a matched retest sensitivity analysis. Stability was assessed using exact agreement and Cohen κ for safety, quadratic-weighted κ for ordinal ratings, and absolute-agreement single-measure intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) for continuous scores and readability indices; 95% CIs used question-level bootstrap resampling. Results: The first round yielded 330 responses. Unsafe responses occurred in every model: ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, and DeepSeek each generated 4 unsafe responses (7.3%); Qwen generated 5 (9.1%); and Doubao generated 6 (10.9%). The overall safety comparison was not statistically significant (Cochran Q=1.909, df=5; P=.86); this finding should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalent safety. Accuracy, empathy, information-quality measures, source-transparency scores, and readability indices differed significantly across models. Across 330 matched question-model pairs, safety classifications agreed in 97.3% of pairs (κ=0.821, 95% CI 0.543-0.979); accuracy and empathy showed weighted κ values of 0.872 and 0.856, respectively; DISCERN (an instrument for judging the quality of written consumer health information on treatment choices) and adapted Ensuring Quality Information for Patients (EQIP) showed ICCs of 0.954 and 0.925. Most readability indices also showed high overall 2-round stability, although model-specific variability remained. Nine safety classifications changed across the 2 rounds (5 from safe to unsafe and 4 from unsafe to safe). Conclusions: In this standardized single-turn COPD question set, model performance differed across several evaluated outcomes, whereas the first-round safety test neither established a between-model difference nor demonstrated equivalence. All 6 models produced potentially unsafe advice, and 9 safety classifications changed between rounds conducted several months apart despite high pooled agreement. These findings support cautious use of LLMs for supplementary COPD education, with clinician oversight for individualized treatment decisions and ongoing reassessment as public-facing systems change.
title: Safety, Accuracy, Empathy, Information Quality, and Readability of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Health Advice Generated by 6 Large Language Models: Cross-Sectional Comparative Evaluation Study

summary: Background: Pharmacoepidemiologic studies using real-world data often lack clinical context embedded in free-text electronic health records (EHRs). However, sharing EHR narratives is restricted by privacy requirements, and conventional deidentification approaches may reduce analytic utility and limit auditability. Objective: This study aims to develop and evaluate a framework that (1) extracts structured cancer-related entities from Japanese EHR free text using BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers)–based natural language processing and (2) generates deidentified analytic text that preserves contextual information for post hoc auditing under privacy constraints. Methods: This retrospective observational study used the DATuM IDEA database, which integrates EHR narratives with structured records (claims, prescriptions, and procedure/surgery records) from 2 hospitals in Japan from January 1, 2019, through June 30, 2025. Deterministic linkage was performed within ICI (Integrated Clinical Care Informatics Inc) prior to deidentification. Downstream recoverability analyses were conducted within a governance-constrained analyzable text cohort derived after deidentification and preprocessing. We quantified deidentification using masking rates and evaluated downstream recoverability of TNM (tumor-node-metastasis) or stage-related mentions, internal logical consistency (M1 vs Stage IV), and proxy-based concordance using structured data treatment proxies (Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical [ATC] code L for systemic anticancer therapy and procedure-name keywords for cancer-directed interventions). A stratified manual audit of 400 deidentified narratives primarily inspected for apparent residual direct identifiers and secondarily for retention of TNM and stage outputs. Results: Among 10,214 patients with neoplasms ( [] C00-D48), linked progress notes were available for 4383 patients (82,863 records). The analyzable text cohort (Layer C) comprised 3689 patients and 38,841 documents, of which 1339 patients (1339/3689, 36.3%) and 11,914 documents (11,914/38,841, 30.7%) had at least one recoverable TNM or stage mention (Layer D). Marginal document-level recoverability in Layer C was 24.2% for T, N, and M elements and 23.6% for stage. Conditional on Layer D, it was 78.8% for T, 78.7% for N, 78.8% for M, and 76.8% for stage. Median masking rates ranged from 9.9% to 15% across major cancer categories. M1 and Stage IV mention indicators showed an overall agreement of 94.7%, positive percent agreement of 54.8%, and negative percent agreement of approximately 99%. Proxy-based concordance analysis showed positive predictive values of 0.700 for Stage IV using the systemic therapy proxy and 0.031 for early-stage classification using the procedure proxy. Manual audit demonstrated retention of intended TNM/stage-related outputs after normalization and identified no apparent residual direct identifiers in the audited deidentified narratives. Conclusions: This framework generates deidentified Japanese EHR narratives that preserve contextual structure for auditing while supporting structured entity extraction, addressing the trade-off between privacy protection and reproducibility in real-world data research.
title: Balancing Privacy Protection and Reproducible Entity Extraction in Real-World Data in the Development of a Framework for Deidentified Japanese Electronic Health Record Narratives Using BERT: Retrospective Observational Study

summary: In "A Machine Learning-Based Model to Predict Overactive Bladder Risk Among US Women: Evidence From the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2011-2018" [1], the authors noted the following corrections. First, the Figure 2B legend has been corrected. Original: “Seven predictor variables corresponding to the log(λ) value with the minimum MSE were retained.” Revised: “Fourteen predictor variables corresponding to the log(λ) value with the minimum MSE (λ = 0.00550) were retained.” At the penalty selected under the minimum criterion (λ = 0.00550), the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) model retained 14 non-zero coefficients, and all 14 variables were entered into model construction. The error was confined to the figure legend text, and no numerical result is affected. Second, the Figure 4A legend has been clarified. The legend now states that Figure 4A displays the 7 continuous predictors among the 14 variables retained by LASSO regression. SHAP beeswarm and dependence plots require a continuous colour gradient and therefore cannot display categorical predictors, which are presented separately; no figure content is affected by this clarification. Third, the sentence reporting the significant predictors in the Results section of the Abstract has been corrected. Original: “Five variables were identified as significant predictors.” Revised: “Five of these 14 variables were identified as the most significant clinical predictors.” Fourth, the sentence characterising the predictive accuracy of the model in the Conclusions has been corrected. Original: “The RF model demonstrated good predictive accuracy and practical clinical applicability, serving as a noninvasive, cost-effective tool for early screening and risk stratification in community health and primary outpatient settings.” Revised: “The RF model demonstrated moderate predictive accuracy and practical clinical applicability, serving as a noninvasive, cost-effective tool for early screening and risk stratification in community health and primary outpatient settings.” These corrections affect the wording of the figure legends, the Abstract, and the Conclusions only. All analyses were performed on the 14 predictors retained by LASSO regression, and every reported metric derives from them; no analytical result is affected. The correction will appear in the online version of the paper on the JMIR Publications website together with the publication of this correction notice. Because this was made after submission to PubMed, PubMed Central, and other full-text repositories, the corrected article has also been resubmitted to those repositories.
title: Correction: A Machine Learning–Based Model to Predict Overactive Bladder Risk Among US Women: Evidence From the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2011-2018

summary: Background: The integration of AI-based Clinical Decision Support Systems (AI-CDSS) into clinical practice has expanded rapidly, particularly in medical imaging. Beyond algorithmic performance, growing evidence suggests that clinicians’ engagement with AI-CDSS is shaped by how transparently systems communicate their outputs, and how trust is formed through human-AI interaction. However, a limited understanding of how these concepts are perceived by end users and developers continues to hinder real-world implementation. Objective: This study aims to explore expert perspectives on transparency and trust in AI-CDSS for chest X-ray diagnosis, with a focus on the two-dimensional lens: user interface and users’ mental models. Methods: A qualitative study was conducted using semistructured interviews with a total of 21 experts, including 11 radiologists and 10 AI experts experienced in AI-CDSS. Data were analyzed thematically to explore factors perceived to influence transparent communication and trust. Results: Three themes emerged: (1) perspective of transparency and trust, (2) user interface, and (3) users’ mental models. Findings reveal that trust is a dynamic calibration process developed through repeated use, feedback loops, and alignment with clinicians’ mental models, rather than algorithmic accuracy alone. Significant discrepancies were identified between how developers design system transparency and how clinicians interpret AI outputs. Conclusions: This study demonstrates that transparency and trust are achieved through interpretable outputs, clear communication of system limitations, and alignment with clinical workflows. Designing trustworthy AI-CDSS requires integrating transparent interface design with consideration of users’ knowledge, experience, and attitudes to support effective human-AI interaction.
title: Expert Perspectives on Transparency and Trust in AI-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems for Chest X-Ray Diagnosis: Qualitative Study

summary: Background: Electronic medical record (EMR) certification programs have traditionally focused on product-level requirements, such as interoperability, security, and core functionality. However, growing evidence suggests that many patient safety risks associated with EMRs arise after implementation and are closely related to system configuration, workflow integration, and real-world use. Despite the presence of a national EMR product certification system in Korea, a systematic evaluation of how certified systems are implemented and used in clinical practice is still lacking. Objective: This study aimed to develop and validate a self-assessment checklist for EMR use certification, focused on patient safety-critical functions, and to evaluate its content validity and expert-assessed practical applicability across health care institutions of different sizes. Methods: A convergent mixed methods design was used. A self-assessment checklist comprising 10 patient safety–related EMR functions was developed by adapting the US Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology self-assessment templates to the Korean EMR certification context. Content validity was quantitatively assessed using the Content Validity Index across 4 dimensions (relevance, usefulness, clarity, and importance) by a panel of 24 experts with experience in EMR implementation and certification. Qualitative feedback was collected through open-ended survey questions to examine feasibility, anticipated challenges, and differentiation between product and use certification across tertiary referral hospitals, general hospitals, and clinics. Results: The overall Scale-Level Content Validity Index was 0.921, indicating strong content validity for the proposed checklist. Although most items demonstrated high agreement, lower ratings were observed for certain functions, particularly in clinic-level settings, reflecting structural and resource-related constraints rather than limited recognition of patient safety priorities. Qualitative findings highlighted challenges related to staffing, system governance, and the feasibility of assembling multidisciplinary assessment teams in smaller institutions. Conclusions: The self-assessment checklist demonstrated high content validity and was perceived as relevant for evaluating patient safety–critical aspects of EMR use. However, expert-assessed feasibility varied across health care institution types, particularly in clinic-level settings. Further empirical testing is needed to assess the checklist’s reliability, usability, and applicability in real-world certification processes.
title: Development and Content Validation of a Self-Assessment Checklist for Electronic Medical Record Use Certification in Korea: Convergent Mixed Methods Study

summary: Background: The administrative burden of manual documentation has been a primary driver of physician burnout and a barrier to patient-centered care. Ambient scribes have emerged as a promising solution that uses passive audio capture and natural language processing to automate clinical note-taking. While their impact on clinical efficiency is frequently studied, there is a lack of research on how these tools have impacted interpersonal communication during clinical encounters. Objective: This study investigates the communication pathways and interactional shifts that occur when ambient scribes are integrated into primary care, with a focus on how physicians adapt their behavior to accommodate an ambient digital listener. Methods: We conducted a qualitative study with 17 licensed family practice physicians in the Greater Toronto Area who use ambient scribes in their daily practice. Data collection included observations from in-person clinical shadowing (n=5) and think-aloud walk-throughs (n=12), each followed by semistructured interviews; reported findings are predominantly drawn from interview data. We analyzed the combined dataset using iterative thematic analysis and open coding to identify affordances and constraints along 3 communication pathways: physician-to-patient, physician-to-patient-and-scribe, and physician-to-note. Results: Along the physician-to-patient pathway, participants reported that ambient scribes increased their capacity to demonstrate active listening, with some reporting greater attentiveness to nonverbal cues, yet introducing the technology to patients to obtain consent consumed limited consultation time, particularly when addressing sensitive health concerns. Along the physician-to-patient-and-scribe pathway, participants appreciated how ambient scribes acted as a forcing function for physicians to verbalize their clinical reasoning to enhance patient comprehension, as well as their scribes’ ability to follow and organize nonlinear conversations. However, they reported that scribes frequently omitted implicit information (eg, deictic gestures) or created unintended documentation artifacts (eg, casual remarks about family members) that required post hoc corrections. Along the physician-to-note pathway, participants reported that scribes optimized their note-taking workflows and enabled note manipulation via spoken words for some physicians but recalling patient information to fix transcription errors and support patient follow-ups proved challenging. Conclusions: Integrating ambient scribes introduces a triadic interactional dynamic into traditionally dyadic patient consultations. Clinicians must continuously navigate the boundaries between patient-facing empathy and scribe-facing precision, deciding when to articulate clinical reasoning aloud and when to exercise verbal discretion regarding sensitive disclosures. While ambient scribes effectively reduce in-encounter computer screen time, they do not eliminate documentation overhead—they redistribute it from real-time typing to postencounter cognitive recall and verbal note curation. To prevent delayed cognitive fatigue from postencounter error verification, we suggest that future ambient scribes should move beyond passive transcription to incorporate interactive recall scaffolding and context-aware error prevention.
title: Impact of Ambient Scribes on Primary Care Communication Pathways: Qualitative Observation and Interview Study
